newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election turning into "duel of the Js".
newsitem.headline: French election turning into "duel of the Js".

text.p: Quite unusually for a French parliamentary election, the campaign for next month's poll is turning into a personal duel between two men -- Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin.

What the French media are calling the "war of the two Js" and the "implacable duel" could climax with a television debate between the two rivals for the premiership before the first round of voting on May 25.
Yet opinion polls show neither man is regarded by his side's supporters as the best candidate for prime minister.

Among conservatives, Juppe came a poor fourth after former prime minister Edouard Balladur, Eurosceptic parliament speaker Philippe Seguin and free-marketeering ex-finance minister Alain Madelin, according to the Ifop poll for the weekly magazine VSD.
Many voters see the balding, abrasive premier, in office since May 1995, as a heartless technocrat despite efforts by "spin doctors" to give him a more human, caring image.
On the left, Jospin narrow trailed former Socialist labour minister Martine Aubry, daughter of former European Commission president Jacques Delors, as the preferred candidate.
Surveys suggest voters see the shy, silver-haired Jospin, defeated but not humiliated by Jacques Chirac in the 1995 presidential election, as decent but dull and out of touch.

The Socialist leader admits that he comes across as stiff and stilted in public, although aides say he is relaxed and has a sense of humour in private. He is an intellectual and lacks a common touch with ordinary voters.
"The personalisation of this combat of chiefs serves both sides mutually, up to a point," wrote commentator Paul Guilbert in the conservative daily Le Figaro.

By rallying behind Juppe, he said, the coalition could at last heal the wounds opened by the 1995 presidential campaign, when Chirac and Balladur, his fellow Gaullist rival, fought a bitter battle that split the right.

Yet the Socialists have homed in on Juppe as a potential coalition liability, attacking his record of tax increases and rising unemployment and painting the election as a referendum on whether voters want five more years of his premiership.
On Wednesday Jospin accused the premier of "aggressiveness". Socialist Party spokesman Francois Hollande said: "Mr Juppe almost physically embodies taxation."
"What does Lionel Jospin really want? Who can tell today what he would do tomorrow if he came to power?" Juppe asked in an anti-Socialist broadside on Tuesday.

In an apparent recognition that some voters could be tempted to cast anti-Juppe protest votes, Francois Baroin, an aide to President Chirac, said the president wanted to "promote a new team" and he alone would choose the next prime minister.
The newspaper Le Figaro, which published Baroin's comments, questioned whether they amounted to "a scoop or a smokescreen".
Juppe himself said in a television interview on Tuesday that his only ambition was to lead the coalition to victory.

But Juppe has been Chirac's closest political associate for more than a decade and the president has stood by him even after he became the most unpopular prime minister in the history of the Fifth Republic last year.
It is hard to imagine that if the coalition won, the president would reward his protege by dumping him.
